guides.title: Scene Safety & MARCH Primary Trauma Survey
steps: Check scene safety first (downed power lines, traffic, fire, venomous animals, structural collapse)—do not become a second casualty.
Run the military/wilderness MARCH assessment in strict priority order so the fastest killers are stopped first:
M — Massive Hemorrhage: Scan head-to-toe for arterial spurting or pooling blood and apply direct pressure, wound packing, or a tourniquet immediately.
A — Airway: Check responsiveness; if unconscious, open airway using head-tilt/chin-lift (or jaw-thrust if neck/spine injury is suspected) and clear visible obstructions.
R — Respiration: Look, listen, and feel for normal breathing for 10 seconds; check chest wall for sucking wounds or uneven rise.
C — Circulation: Check radial/carotid pulse, pale/clammy skin, and treat for shock by laying flat and keeping warm.

H — Hypothermia / Head Injury: Insulate from cold ground immediately (even injured patients in warm climates go hypothermic from blood loss) and note pupil equality and mental orientation (AVPU: Alert, Verbal, Pain, Unresponsive).
guides.safety: Always put on nitrile gloves before touching blood or bodily fluids.

guides.title: Adult, Child & Infant Hands-Only & Rescue CPR
steps: Tap shoulders firmly and shout; if unresponsive and not breathing normally (gasping/agonal breaths are NOT normal breathing), yell for someone to call 911 and bring an AED.
Place person flat on their back on a firm surface; kneel beside chest and place heel of one hand on the center of the lower half of the breastbone (sternum) with your other hand locked on top.

Push hard and fast at 100–120 compressions per minute ('Stayin' Alive' tempo) to a depth of 2–2.4 inches (about 1.5 inches for infants using 2 fingers/thumbs), allowing full chest recoil between pushes.
If trained and equipped with a barrier mask (and for drowning, drug overdose, or children), give 30 compressions followed by 2 gentle 1-second breaths just enough to make the chest rise.
Turn on the AED as soon as it arrives, apply pads to bare dry chest as pictured, clear everyone during rhythm analysis and shock, and immediately resume compressions.
guides.safety: Do not stop chest compressions for more than 10 seconds at any time until paramedics take over or the person wakes up.

guides.title: Choking Relief: Heimlich Abdominal Thrusts & Infant Back Blows
steps: If the person can cough forcefully or speak, encourage them to keep coughing—do NOT slap their back while upright.

If unable to speak, cough, or breathe (universal hands-at-throat sign): stand behind them, wrap arms around waist, make a fist with thumb side inward just above the navel and well below the breastbone, grasp fist with other hand, and deliver sharp inward-and-upward J-thrusts until the object expels.
For pregnant or large-abdomen individuals: place fists on the center of the breastbone and perform straight-back chest thrusts.

For infants under 1 year: support baby face-down along your forearm with head lower than chest, deliver 5 firm back blows between shoulder blades with heel of hand, flip face-up, and give 5 two-finger chest compressions; repeat.
Self-Heimlich when alone: drive your upper abdomen forcefully over the back of a sturdy chair, porch railing, or kitchen counter edge.
guides.safety: If a choking victim loses consciousness, lower them gently to the floor and start CPR immediately, checking the mouth for the object before giving breaths.

guides.title: Recognizing & Treating Hypovolemic / Circulatory Shock
steps: Watch for early shock signs after injury, blood loss, severe burns, or dehydration: rapid weak pulse, pale/cool/clammy skin, rapid shallow breathing, anxiety/confusion, nausea, and extreme thirst.
Control all external bleeding first.
Lay the person flat on their back (unless having trouble breathing or suspected head/neck injury) and elevate legs 6–12 inches if no leg/pelvis fractures exist.
Slide an insulated pad or folded blankets UNDERNEATH them and wrap them warmly—shock destroys the body's ability to regulate temperature even in warm weather.
Loosen tight belts/collars, reassure calmly, and do NOT give food or large amounts of water if surgery may be needed or if drowsy/nauseated.
guides.safety: Never wait for low blood pressure to treat shock—by the time blood pressure drops, shock is already critical.

guides.title: Recovery Position & Managing Unconscious Breathing Patients
steps: Use the recovery position for any unconscious person who is breathing normally and has NO suspected neck or spine injury—it prevents the tongue or vomit from blocking the airway.
Kneel beside them, place the arm nearest you at a right angle with palm up, and bring their far arm across their chest holding the back of their hand against their near cheek.
Grasp their far knee, pull it up until the foot is flat, and roll them smoothly toward you onto their side.
Tilt their head slightly back to keep the airway open and check breathing every 2 minutes.
guides.safety: If a head, neck, or back injury is suspected (fall, car crash, diving), keep the head and spine aligned in place unless vomit threatens the airway.

guides.title: Anaphylaxis Recognition & Epinephrine Auto-Injector (EpiPen) Use
steps: Recognize severe allergic anaphylaxis (from bee stings, fire ants, shellfish, peanuts, medications): throat tightness, hoarse voice, wheezing, lip/tongue swelling, widespread hives, dizziness/fainting, or vomiting.

Remove the safety cap, hold firmly in a fist ('blue to the sky, orange to the thigh'), and press firmly against the outer mid-thigh (works straight through jeans/pants) until it clicks; hold for 3–10 seconds per device instructions.
Call 911 immediately and have the person lie flat with legs elevated (or sit upright if struggling to breathe)—do NOT let them stand or walk suddenly, which can trigger fatal blood-pressure collapse.
If symptoms do not improve or return after 5–15 minutes (biphasic reaction), administer a second auto-injector in the opposite thigh.
guides.safety: Antihistamines (Benadryl) are too slow to stop anaphylaxis—epinephrine is the ONLY life-saving first-line treatment.

guides.title: Heart Attack vs. Stroke (BE-FAST) Recognition & Immediate Action
supplies: Regular uncoated 325 mg aspirin (or four 81 mg baby aspirins)
steps: Heart Attack signs: chest pressure/squeezing/fullness, pain radiating to left arm, jaw, neck, or back, cold sweat, shortness of breath, or unusual fatigue/nausea (especially in women).
Call 911 immediately, sit the person upright at rest, and have them CHEW (not swallow whole) one 325 mg uncoated aspirin unless allergic or actively bleeding.

Stroke BE-FAST check: Balance loss sudden; Eyes blurry/double; Face drooping on one side when smiling; Arm drifting downward when both raised; Speech slurred/confused; Time to call 911 immediately and note the exact minute symptoms started (clot-busting drugs have a strict 3–4.5 hour window).
guides.safety: NEVER give aspirin for a suspected stroke—15% of strokes are hemorrhagic (brain bleeds) where aspirin worsens bleeding.

guides.title: Diabetic Emergencies: Hypoglycemia (Low Blood Sugar) Rule of 15
supplies: Glucose tablets, 4 oz regular fruit juice/soda, or 1 tbsp honey/sugar
steps: Recognize low blood sugar (shaking, sweating, irritability, confusion, slurred speech—often mistaken for drunkenness); when in doubt between high and low blood sugar, always treat as LOW because low sugar kills within minutes.
If awake and able to swallow safely, give 15 grams of fast-acting sugar (4 glucose tablets, 4 oz regular juice/soda, or 1 tbsp honey) using the Rule of 15.
Wait 15 minutes and recheck; if still under 70 mg/dL or symptomatic, repeat another 15 grams of fast sugar, then follow with protein + complex carbs (crackers with peanut butter).
If unconscious or unable to swallow, do NOT force liquids into the mouth—place in recovery position, administer nasal/injectable glucagon if available, and call 911.
guides.safety: Never give diet soda or chocolate/candy bars first—fat in chocolate slows sugar absorption.

guides.title: Stop-the-Bleed: Direct Pressure, Wound Packing & Tourniquets
steps: Expose the wound immediately with trauma shears so you see the exact bleeding source.

For non-limb wounds (neck, armpit, groin) or deep extremity lacerations: pack hemostatic or plain gauze tightly all the way down onto the bleeding vessel at the bottom of the wound cavity, then hold continuous firm two-handed pressure for 3–5 full minutes without peeking.

For life-threatening bright-red spurting or pooling arm/leg bleeding: apply a commercial windlass tourniquet 2–3 inches ABOVE the wound (never over a joint) or 'high and tight' near the armpit/groin, pull the strap tight, twist the windlass rod until bright red bleeding stops completely, lock the rod in the clip, and write the exact application time on the strap.
guides.safety: Once applied for arterial bleeding, NEVER loosen or remove a tourniquet in the field—leave removal to hospital surgeons.

guides.title: Improvised Windlass Tourniquet (When Commercial Gear Is Absent)
gear: Sturdy hardwood stick, wrench, or metal spoon (windlass)
supplies: 2-inch-wide non-stretch cloth band (triangular bandage, torn shirt strip, belt—NEVER wire, shoelace, or thin cord)
steps: Cut or fold a strong, non-elastic fabric strip at least 2 inches wide (narrow cord cuts into flesh and nerves without compressing deep arteries).
Wrap the cloth band twice around the limb 2–3 inches above the wound and tie a single overhand knot.
Place a rigid stick or heavy metal spoon on top of the knot and tie a full square knot over the stick.
Twist the stick like a propeller until arterial bleeding stops completely, then tie the ends of the stick down against the limb with a second cloth strip so it cannot unwind.
guides.safety: Expect a properly tightened tourniquet to be painful—do not back off twisting just because it hurts if bright red bleeding continues.

guides.title: Sucking Chest Wound & Vented Chest Seal Application
supplies: Vented commercial chest seal (HyFin) OR heavy plastic sheet + medical/duct tape
steps: Recognize an open chest wound (gunshot, stab, impalement): air sucking/bubbling through the chest wall, frothy pink sputum, or worsening shortness of breath.
Wipe blood/sweat off the chest skin quickly, have the patient exhale fully, and slap a vented chest seal directly over the wound (check the back/armpits for an exit wound and seal that too).

If using improvised plastic (cut zip-top bag or wrapper) with no commercial seal: tape all 4 sides down, OR tape 3 sides leaving the bottom corner open as a flutter valve so trapped air escapes on exhale without sucking in on inhale.
Watch closely for tension pneumothorax (worsening breathing, bulging neck veins, blue lips): if using a homemade 4-sided seal, briefly lift one corner during exhalation to burp trapped air.
guides.safety: Keep the patient sitting slightly upright or leaning onto their injured side so the healthy lung can expand freely.

guides.title: Impaled Objects & Abdominal Evisceration Field Care
supplies: Clean plastic wrap / moist sterile dressings
steps: Impaled Object (knife, rebar, glass, branch): NEVER pull the object out—it acts as a plug preventing catastrophic internal hemorrhage (only exception: an object through the cheek blocking the airway).
Cut clothing away around the object, build bulky doughnut-shaped pads of rolled gauze around the base on all sides, and tape firmly to stabilize the object from wobbling during transport.

Abdominal Evisceration (protruding organs): Do NOT push organs back inside; cover gently with sterile dressings soaked in clean warm saline/water, cover with plastic wrap to lock in moisture and warmth, and bend knees slightly to relax abdominal muscles.
guides.safety: Keep impaled limbs completely immobilized and seek immediate surgical evacuation.

guides.title: Wound Irrigation, Steri-Strip Closure & Infection Prevention
gear: 60 mL irrigation syringe (or clean zip-top bag with pinhole)
supplies: Drinkable clean water or sterile saline
steps: Stop bleeding first, then wash hands and flush the wound forcefully with at least 500 mL–1 liter of clean drinkable water using an irrigation syringe—high-volume water pressure is the #1 way to prevent infection.

Wash surrounding skin with mild soap and pick out visible dirt/gravel with alcohol-wiped tweezers (avoid pouring harsh rubbing alcohol or hydrogen peroxide straight into deep raw tissue, which kills healing cells).
For clean, shallow straight cuts under 1 inch where edges meet easily: dry surrounding skin, apply Steri-Strips across the cut starting at the center to pull edges gently together without puckering.
Keep moist with plain petroleum jelly or bacitracin under a clean bandage changed daily—moist wounds heal 2x faster with less scarring than dry scabs.
guides.safety: NEVER glue or tape shut deep puncture wounds, animal/human bites, dirty jagged wounds, or cuts older than 6–8 hours—trapping bacteria inside causes severe abscesses.

guides.title: Severe Nosebleeds (Epistaxis) & Knocked-Out Tooth Rescue
steps: Nosebleed: Sit upright and lean SLIGHTLY FORWARD (never tilt head back, which sends blood down the throat causing vomiting) and pinch the soft lower nostrils firmly together against the septum for 10–15 continuous minutes without releasing.
Apply a cold compress across the bridge of the nose (optional: 2 sprays of Afrin nasal decongestant constricts bleeding vessels rapidly).

Knocked-Out Adult Tooth (30-minute critical window): Pick up the tooth ONLY by the white crown—NEVER touch or scrub the root; rinse gently in milk or saliva if dirty, push back into the socket gently and bite on gauze, OR store submerged in cold whole milk or inside the cheek until reaching a dentist within 30–60 minutes.
guides.safety: Never re-implant a knocked-out baby tooth (can damage the permanent tooth bud underneath).

guides.title: Eye Injuries: Chemical Splash Flushing & Foreign Object Removal
gear: Clean pitcher / water bottle / eye wash cup
supplies: Clean lukewarm water or sterile saline
steps: Chemical Splash (bleach, pool acid, cleaner): Flush the open eye immediately with continuous gentle lukewarm water for at least 15–20 minutes, tilting head so runoff drains from the inner nose corner outward away from the uninjured eye.
Loose Eyelash/Dust: Pull upper eyelid gently down over the lower lashes so tears flush it out, or rinse with clean saline.

Embedded Metal/Wood/Glass in Eye: Do NOT rub or try to pull it out; tape a stiff paper cup or protective shield over the injured eye and cover the uninjured eye lightly (both eyes move together) to stop eye movement during transport.
guides.safety: Contact lenses must be removed gently as soon as chemical flushing begins.

guides.title: Fishhook Removal (String-Yank Method) & Splinter / Blister Care
gear: Heavy braided fishing line or 550 paracord inner strand
steps: Fishhook String-Yank (only for single-barb hooks NOT near eyes, face, arteries, or joints): Loop a 2-ft piece of strong line around the curve of the hook, press the eye of the hook flat against the skin with one finger to disengage the barb, and give one sharp, swift yank parallel to the skin.
Alternative advance-and-cut method: push the barb completely through the skin, snip the barb off with wire cutters, and back the smooth shank out.
Friction Blisters: Do NOT pop intact blisters (roof skin is a sterile natural bandage); cut a doughnut-shaped ring of moleskin around the blister or cover directly with a hydrocolloid bandage.
guides.safety: Verify tetanus vaccination is up to date (within 5 years for dirty puncture/hook wounds).

guides.title: SAM Splint & Improvised Splinting (Joint Above & Joint Below)
supplies: Elastic wrap (ACE bandage) or triangular bandages
steps: Check CSM (Circulation, Sensation, Motion) distal to the injury BEFORE and AFTER splinting: feel pulse, check capillary refill (<2 seconds), and ask patient to wiggle fingers/toes.
Curve a SAM splint into a C-gutter or T-beam fold—bending flat aluminum foam multiplies its structural rigidity 10x.
Immobilize the bone AND the joint above and joint below the fracture (for a forearm break, splint from fingertips past the elbow).
Pad all bony hollows (wrist, elbow, ankle) with soft cloth and wrap snug—never tight enough to numb fingers or turn nails blue.
guides.safety: If a deformed fracture has zero distal pulse and help is hours away, apply gentle inline traction once to restore blood flow; otherwise splint in the position found.

guides.title: Ankle & Knee Sprains: PEACE & LOVE Protocol & Field Taping
steps: Check Ottawa Ankle Rules to rule out fracture: if the person cannot bear weight for 4 steps OR has sharp bone tenderness on the back edge of either ankle bone (malleolus), splint as a fracture.

For soft-tissue sprains: Protect (unload 1–3 days), Elevate above heart level when resting, Avoid excessive anti-inflammatories in the first 48 hours if mild (natural inflammation starts tissue repair), Compress gently with an elastic figure-8 wrap starting from the toes upward.
If forced to hike out on a mild ankle sprain, leave the boot ON for support and wrap a figure-8 ankle lock over the boot with athletic tape or triangular bandage.
guides.safety: Loosen compression wraps immediately if throbbing pain, tingling, or cold toes develop.

guides.title: Head Injury / Concussion Red Flags & Spinal Immobilization
steps: Suspect spinal injury after any high-impact fall, diving accident, or vehicle crash: hold the head steady in neutral inline position with both hands and pack rolled jackets/packs on both sides so the neck cannot turn.

Monitor concussion patients every 30 minutes for emergency brain-bleed red flags: worsening severe headache, repeated vomiting, unequal pupil sizes, slurred speech, confusion/combativeness, clear fluid/blood from ears or nose, or inability to stay awake.
Do NOT give aspirin or ibuprofen for a fresh head injury (increases intracranial bleeding risk).
guides.safety: Any loss of consciousness, amnesia, or unequal pupils requires immediate emergency evacuation.

guides.title: Thermal Burns (1st, 2nd & 3rd Degree) & Rule of Nines
supplies: Non-stick sterile dressings / clean plastic wrap
steps: Stop the burning process immediately and cool the burn under cool (NOT ice-cold) running water for 15–20 minutes—never apply ice, butter, grease, or toothpaste.
Remove rings, watches, and tight clothing BEFORE swelling traps them (leave fabric stuck to deep burns intact and cut around it).
Estimate burn size using the Rule of Nines (adult arm = 9%, front torso = 18%, back torso = 18%, each leg = 18%, head = 9%; patient's palm = ~1%).

Cover 2nd-degree blisters and 3rd-degree white/charred burns loosely with sterile non-stick gauze or clean kitchen plastic wrap to block air pain and infection; seek emergency care for any 3rd-degree burn, burns >10% body area, or burns on face, hands, feet, groin, or major joints.
guides.safety: Never pop burn blisters or put ice directly on burned skin, which causes frostbite tissue necrosis.

guides.title: Electrical Burns & Chemical Powder/Liquid Burn Protocol
steps: Electrical Shock/Burn: NEVER touch the victim until power is shut off at the breaker/switch or the live wire is moved with a dry non-conductive wooden/plastic pole; check breathing/CPR immediately and look for BOTH entry and exit burns (internal muscle damage is far worse than surface marks).
Dry Chemical Powder (lime, cement, lye): Brush dry powder off skin and clothes completely BEFORE flushing with water (water activates dry lime/lye into caustic heat).
Liquid Chemical Burn: Flush continuously with copious running water for 20+ minutes while removing contaminated clothing.
guides.safety: All electrical shocks require medical ECG evaluation even if surface skin looks minor.

guides.title: Shoulder Dislocation & Nursemaid's Elbow Field Reduction
steps: Anterior Shoulder Dislocation (arm held slightly out, squared-off shoulder contour): Check wrist pulse and thumb sensation first.

Stimson Gravity Technique (safest gentle field method when hours from a hospital): Have the patient lie face-down on a bench/ledge with the injured arm hanging straight down vertically, strap a 5–10 lb weight (water bag/pack) to the wrist, and let muscles relax for 15–20 minutes until the humeral head glides back into the socket.
Once reduced (or if unable to reduce), immobilize the arm across the chest in a sling and horizontal swathe bandage.
guides.safety: Never yank or lever a dislocated shoulder forcefully—brachial plexus nerves and axillary arteries run directly under the joint.

guides.title: Heat Exhaustion vs. Life-Threatening Heat Stroke (Rapid Cooling)
steps: Distinguish quickly: Heat Exhaustion = heavy sweating, weakness, dizziness, nausea, normal mental clarity. Heat Stroke = core temp >104°F PLUS central nervous system dysfunction (confusion, slurred speech, staggering, seizures, or collapse; skin may be red/dry OR still drenched in sweat).

Heat Stroke is a 30-minute medical emergency ('Cool First, Transport Second'): call 911 and immediately immerse the person up to the neck in an ice-water bath/kiddie pool, OR use the Tarp-Assisted Cooling (TACO) method—lay them on a tarp, lift edges, and pour gallons of ice water over them continuously.
If ice immersion isn't available, pack ice/cold wet towels at the neck, armpits, and groin while spraying mist and fanning aggressively.
For mild Heat Exhaustion (alert, no vomiting): move to AC/shade, loosen clothing, and sip cool electrolyte solution slowly.
guides.safety: Never force liquids into a confused or semi-conscious heat-stroke patient.

guides.title: Hypothermia Stages & Safe Rewarming (Preventing Afterdrop)
steps: Mild Hypothermia (95°F–90°F — shivering, clumsy fingers 'the umbles': mumbles, stumbles, fumbles): Get out of wind/wet, strip wet clothes inside shelter, insulate from ground, put in dry sleeping bag, and give warm high-sugar fluids.

Severe Hypothermia (<90°F — shivering STOPS, rigid muscles, confusion/apathy, very slow pulse): Handle GENTLY (rough jostling triggers fatal heart arrhythmia/ventricular fibrillation), keep horizontal, and wrap in a 'hypothermia burrito' (tarp + sleeping bag + warm water bottles wrapped in socks placed on chest/armpits/groin—NEVER on arms/legs).
Do NOT put a severely hypothermic person in a hot shower or rub their limbs—that rushes cold peripheral blood back to the heart ('afterdrop').
guides.safety: Check pulse for a full 60 seconds in severe hypothermia before starting CPR, as heart rate may be 10–15 beats/minute.

guides.title: Frostbite & Immersion (Trench) Foot Field Treatment
steps: Frostnip (pale, cold, tingling skin still soft): Rewarm immediately via skin-to-skin contact (tucking fingers in armpits).
Deep Frostbite (waxy white/greyish-blue hard frozen tissue): Do NOT thaw if there is ANY chance the limb could refreeze before reaching definitive shelter (refreezing destroys tissue permanently).

Once safely indoors, immerse the frostbitten part in circulating warm water strictly between 99°F and 102°F (test with an uninjured elbow—never hot water or near a fire) for 20–30 minutes until flushed and pliable, place dry sterile gauze between toes/fingers, and give ibuprofen.
guides.safety: Never rub frostbitten skin with snow or hands—ice crystals inside cells shred tissue.

guides.title: Near-Drowning Rescue & Secondary Dry-Drowning Observation
gear: Throw rope / flotation ring / long pole
steps: Follow Reach-Throw-Row-Go: extend a pole/paddle or throw a floating cooler/life ring from shore first—panicked drowning victims pull untrained swimmers underwater.
Once out of water, check breathing immediately; if not breathing, start CPR starting with 2 rescue breaths (drowning is an oxygen-starvation arrest) followed by 30 compressions.
Expect water/vomit regurgitation—turn the head/body to the side to clear the airway and resume CPR.

Every near-drowning survivor who inhaled water MUST be observed in an ER or watched closely for 24 hours for delayed pulmonary edema (persistent coughing, chest pain, fast breathing, extreme fatigue).
guides.safety: Drowning is silent—victims cannot wave or shout because their airway is fighting for breath.

guides.title: Altitude Sickness (AMS, HAPE & HACE) Prevention & Descent Rule
steps: Ascend gradually above 8,000 ft (no more than 1,000–1,600 ft sleeping elevation gain per day) and stay well hydrated.
Acute Mountain Sickness (AMS — throbbing headache, nausea, dizziness, insomnia): Stop ascending, rest, hydrate, and take ibuprofen or acetazolamide.

Life-threatening HACE (ataxia/stumbling like drunk, confusion) or HAPE (gurgling cough, pink frothy sputum, breathless at rest): DESCEND immediately at least 1,500–3,000 feet—descent is the only definitive cure.
guides.safety: Never ascend with unresolved AMS symptoms, and never leave a sick teammate alone to descend.

guides.title: Stingray Barb Injury: Hot-Water Immersion & Spine Protocol
supplies: Hot water (110°F–113°F — as hot as tolerable without scalding)
steps: Always shuffle your feet ('stingray shuffle') when wading in warm Gulf Coast surf (Galveston/Surfside) so rays swim away instead of whipping their barbed tail.

If stung (usually ankle/foot): get out of the water, control bleeding with gentle direct pressure, and IMMEDIATELY submerge the wound in hot water (110°F–113°F / 43°C–45°C) for 30 to 90 minutes—heat denatures the heat-labile protein venom and stops agonizing pain within minutes.
Remove loose superficial spine fragments with tweezers, ONLY if protruding easily—NEVER pull out a deeply embedded barb in the chest, abdomen, neck, or near a major joint/artery.

Irrigate thoroughly with clean water and seek urgent medical care: stingray barbs shred tissue and carry marine Vibrio/Aeromonas bacteria requiring X-rays (to check for retained sheath fragments), tetanus update, and marine-specific antibiotics (doxycycline/ciprofloxacin).
guides.safety: Test hot water on your own uninjured hand first so a numb/shocked victim doesn't get scalded; NEVER pack a stingray wound in ice (cold locks in the venom and intensifies pain).

guides.title: Jellyfish & Portuguese Man-of-War Stings (Vinegar vs. Seawater)
steps: Get out of the water immediately and do NOT rub the skin with towels, sand, or bare hands—friction triggers millions of unfired microscopic nematocyst venom darts.

Douse the area generously with household white vinegar for at least 30 seconds to neutralize unfired stinging cells (for Atlantic/Gulf jellyfish & Box Jellyfish; if no vinegar is handy, rinse with SEAWATER only—NEVER use freshwater, urine, or rubbing alcohol, which cause osmotic firing of remaining stingers).
Pluck off visible tentacles with tweezers or scrape gently with the edge of a credit card after vinegar deactivation.
Relieve residual pain by soaking in hot water (110°F–113°F) for 20–40 minutes (or applying an ice pack wrapped in cloth if hot water isn't available) and apply 1% hydrocortisone cream.
guides.safety: Call 911 immediately if stings cover a large area or cause chest tightness, breathing trouble, muscle cramps, or dizziness (Irukandji / Man-of-War systemic reaction).

guides.title: Sea Urchin Spines, Catfish Fin Punctures & Vibrio Wound Alert
steps: Hardhead Catfish / Gafftopsail Fin Puncture (common in Gulf bays/piers) & Sea Urchin Spines: Submerge the punctured hand/foot in hot water (110°F–113°F) for 30–60 minutes to neutralize venom proteins and ease throbbing pain.
Remove large visible spines straight out with tweezers without snapping brittle urchin tips off under the skin (soaking in vinegar helps dissolve tiny superficial calcium spines).
Flush forcefully with clean freshwater and monitor closely for 48 hours for redness, warmth, or red streaks.
guides.safety: GULF COAST VIBRIO WARNING: Any cut, scrape, or puncture exposed to warm brackish bay/gulf water that develops rapid swelling, blistering, fever, or severe pain within 12–48 hours requires IMMEDIATE emergency IV antibiotics.

guides.title: North American Pit Viper Bites (Rattlesnake, Copperhead, Cottonmouth)
steps: Move safely away from the snake (snakes can strike up to half their body length), keep the victim completely calm and still, and call 911 / Poison Control (1-800-222-1222).
Remove rings, watches, bracelets, and tight boots IMMEDIATELY before rapid swelling begins.
Keep the bitten limb immobilized at or slightly below heart level (neutral position) and trace the leading edge of swelling with a pen every 15 minutes with the time written beside it.

STRICTLY DO NOT: cut the wound, suck out venom, use a venom extractor pump, apply ice, apply a tight tourniquet, or give alcohol/aspirin/ibuprofen (CroFab antivenom at the hospital is the only effective treatment).
guides.safety: Even a decapitated snake head can reflex-bite and inject venom for up to an hour—never handle a dead snake.

guides.title: Coral Snake Bites & Pressure-Immobilization Bandage
steps: Recognize North American Coral Snakes (Texas/Southeast): 'Red on yellow, kill a fellow; red on black, venom lack' (Note: coral snakes have black snouts and small fixed fangs that chew rather than strike, often leaving minimal initial pain/swelling before neurotoxic paralysis starts hours later).
Call 911 immediately—neurotoxic venom can paralyze diaphragm breathing muscles.

For neurotoxic elapid bites (Coral snakes, cobras, sea snakes): wrap a wide elastic bandage firmly (like a sprained ankle wrap, NOT cutting off pulse) starting over the bite and wrapping all the way up the limb, then splint the limb still.
guides.safety: Do NOT use tight pressure-immobilization wraps on Pit Vipers (rattlesnakes/copperheads), as trapping tissue-destroying hemotoxin in one spot worsens local necrosis.

guides.title: Black Widow & Brown Recluse Spider Bites
steps: Wash the bite site gently with soap and water and apply a cloth-wrapped ice pack for 15 minutes on / 15 minutes off to slow venom spread and relieve pain.

Black Widow (shiny black with red hourglass; neurotoxin): Watch for severe abdominal/back muscle cramps, sweating, nausea, and high blood pressure within 1–6 hours—seek hospital care for muscle relaxants/antivenom.

Brown Recluse (violin-shaped mark on cephalothorax; necrotoxin): Elevate the limb, keep cool, avoid heat pads (heat accelerates enzyme tissue breakdown), and see a doctor if a dark purple 'bull's-eye' blister or ulcer develops over 24–72 hours.
guides.safety: Shake out gardening gloves, garage shoes, and stored blankets before putting them on.

guides.title: Tick Removal, Lyme / Rocky Mountain Spotted Fever & Chiggers
steps: Grasp the tick with fine-tipped tweezers as close to the skin's surface as possible (by the head/mouthparts, NEVER squeezing the swollen belly).
Pull straight upward with steady, even pressure—do NOT twist or jerk, which snaps mouthparts off in the skin.
NEVER apply petroleum jelly, nail polish, rubbing alcohol, or a hot match to a live attached tick—suffocating a tick causes it to regurgitate infectious saliva straight into your bloodstream.
Clean the bite with rubbing alcohol/soap, save the tick in a dated bag/tape card, and watch for 30 days for a bull's-eye rash, fever, body aches, or spotted wrist/ankle rash.
guides.safety: Prompt removal within 24 hours dramatically reduces Lyme disease transmission.

guides.title: Bee, Wasp, Fire Ant & Scorpion Stings + Asp Caterpillar
supplies: Baking soda paste (1 tbsp baking soda + water)
steps: Honeybee: Scrape the barbed venom sac sideways out of the skin immediately with a fingernail or credit card—never pinch the sac with tweezers, which squeezes the remaining venom in.

Fire Ants (Texas): Brush off ants rapidly, wash with soap/water, apply a cold compress and baking soda paste or 1% hydrocortisone cream, and leave white pustules intact (popping causes secondary staph infection).

Puss Caterpillar ('Asp' — furry teardrop caterpillar dropping from Texas oaks): Press sticky cellophane/duct tape onto the sting and rip off repeatedly to pull out embedded venomous spines before washing.
Scorpion: Wash, apply a cool compress, take acetaminophen/ibuprofen, and monitor children closely for involuntary eye movements or muscle twitching.
guides.safety: Watch every sting victim for 30 minutes for throat swelling, hives, or wheezing (anaphylaxis).

guides.title: Poison Ivy, Oak & Sumac: Urushiol Oil Wash-Off & Rash Remedies
steps: Memorize 'Leaves of three, let it be' (poison ivy climbs hairy vines or grows as a low shrub; poison sumac has 7–13 smooth leaflets in wet bogs).

You have a 30-to-60-minute golden window after brushing the plant to prevent a rash completely: wash exposed skin with dish soap (Dawn) and a WET WASHCLOTH using firm friction in cool water (urushiol binds like invisible axle grease—soap without washcloth friction leaves oil behind; hot water opens pores).
Wash all clothes, boots, tools, and pet fur that touched the plant—urushiol stays active on gear and boots for up to 5 years.
For an active itchy rash: use cool colloidal oatmeal baths, calamine lotion, cool compresses, and oral antihistamines at night (blister fluid itself does NOT spread the rash).
guides.safety: NEVER burn poison ivy vines in a brush pile or campfire—inhaling aerosolized urushiol smoke causes life-threatening lung inflammation.

guides.title: Ingested Poisons, Activated Charcoal Rules & Poison Control Protocol
supplies: Activated charcoal powder/liquid (ONLY when directed by Poison Control)
steps: Call Poison Control immediately (US: 1-800-222-1222 — free, 24/7, staffed by toxicology nurses/pharmacists) with the exact container, amount swallowed, victim's weight, and time of ingestion.

NEVER induce vomiting (no ipecac, salt water, or finger-down-throat)—vomiting caustic cleaners/bleach burns the esophagus a second time, and vomiting hydrocarbons (gasoline, lamp oil) causes fatal chemical pneumonia.

Activated Charcoal (25–50 g adult dose mixed in water): Effective ONLY within 1 hour of swallowing certain pill/plant overdoses AND ONLY if the person is wide awake and alert—charcoal does NOT bind acids, alkalis, bleach, gasoline, alcohols, iron, or lithium.
For skin or eye poison contact, strip contaminated clothing and flush with water for 15–20 minutes while calling Poison Control.
guides.safety: Never give activated charcoal to a drowsy or vomiting patient—aspirating charcoal into the lungs can be fatal.

guides.title: Carbon Monoxide & Smoke Inhalation Poisoning Rescue
steps: Recognize Carbon Monoxide (CO) poisoning during storms/winter outages (from generators, grills, or blocked vents): simultaneous dull headache, dizziness, nausea, confusion, and flu-like fatigue across multiple people or pets in the house.
Get every person and pet out into fresh outdoor air IMMEDIATELY, leave doors open, and call 911.

For smoke inhalation in a fire: check for singed nose hairs, soot around mouth/nostrils, or hoarse voice—these signal airway swelling that can close the windpipe within hours and require hospital oxygen/airway monitoring.
guides.safety: Ordinary pulse oximeters read falsely normal (98%–100%) during carbon monoxide poisoning because they cannot distinguish CO from oxygen on hemoglobin.

guides.title: Animal & Human Bite Wound Care & Rabies / Tetanus Protocol
steps: Control active bleeding with direct pressure, then scrub and irrigate the bite aggressively with soap and copious running water for 10–15 minutes to flush out saliva and bacteria.

Leave puncture-type animal or human bites OPEN (cover loosely with sterile gauze)—cat bites and human clenched-fist bites carry Pasteurella and anaerobic bacteria that cause rapid deep-space infections if stitched closed.

Seek medical care within 8 hours for prophylactic antibiotics (amoxicillin-clavulanate), tetanus booster, and rabies post-exposure evaluation (especially after bat, raccoon, skunk, fox, or stray bite—note a bat inside a bedroom with a sleeping person warrants rabies evaluation even without a visible bite mark).
guides.safety: Do not attempt to capture a wild animal bare-handed—note its description and direction of travel for animal control.

guides.title: WHO Oral Rehydration Salts (ORS) Homemade Ratio for Severe Diarrhea/Vomiting
steps: Dehydration from gastroenteritis, cholera, or heat illness is the #1 preventable killer in disasters—plain water alone is poorly absorbed when the gut is inflamed.

Mix the exact World Health Organization ratio: dissolve 6 level teaspoons of sugar and 1/2 level teaspoon of salt into 1 liter (1 quart) of clean safe water until crystal clear (taste check: it should taste no saltier than tears).
Administer in small frequent sips (1 tablespoon every 5 minutes) even if vomiting—small sips absorb through the stomach lining without triggering stretch vomiting.
Discard unused solution after 24 hours (or 48 hours if refrigerated).
guides.safety: Measure salt precisely—too much salt worsens dehydration and causes hypernatremia.

guides.title: Recognizing Sepsis, Cellulitis & Spreading Wound Infections
steps: Normal wound healing shows mild pinkness within 1/4-inch of cut edges that fades after Day 2.

Infection signs (Days 2–5): expanding redness, throbbing warmth, swelling, pus, and red streaks moving up the limb toward lymph nodes (lymphangitis)—trace the outer border of redness with a pen and write the time.

Sepsis Emergency Warning (TIME): Temperature >100.4°F or <96.8°F; Infection signs; Mental decline (confusion, extreme sleepiness); Extremely ill (fast heart rate >90, rapid breathing >22, mottled/clammy skin)—requires immediate emergency hospital IV antibiotics.
guides.safety: Never squeeze or lance deep facial boils or red-streaking infections in the field.

guides.title: Fever Management: Safe Acetaminophen / Ibuprofen Alternating & Sponge Cooling
steps: Remember fever itself is an immune defense—treat discomfort rather than chasing a magic number unless temp exceeds 103°F–104°F or in infants/elderly.

For high stubborn adult fevers, alternate Acetaminophen (500–650 mg every 6 hours; strict max 3,000–4,000 mg/24 hrs) and Ibuprofen (400–600 mg every 6 hours with food; max 2,400 mg/24 hrs) staggered 3 hours apart—log every dose time on paper.
Use lukewarm (NOT cold) sponge baths and light breathable sheets—ice baths or rubbing alcohol rubs cause shivering that actually drives core temperature HIGHER.
guides.safety: NEVER give aspirin to children or teenagers with viral fevers (risk of fatal Reye's syndrome), and check cold/flu combo pills so you don't double-dose acetaminophen.

guides.title: Evidence-Based Herbal & Kitchen Remedies (Honey, Ginger, Peppermint, Garlic, Plantain)
steps: 1. Cough & Sore Throat: Take 1–2 teaspoons of raw buckwheat or wildflower honey straight (clinically proven equal or superior to OTC dextromethorphan for nighttime cough) + warm salt-water gargle (1/2 tsp salt in 8 oz warm water).
2. Nausea & Motion Sickness: Simmer 5–6 thin slices of fresh ginger root in 1 cup water for 10 minutes and sip slowly.
3. Indigestion, Gas & Tension Headache: Steep peppermint tea for gut cramps; rub diluted peppermint essential oil (2 drops in 1 tsp carrier oil) on temples for tension headaches.

4. Insect Bites & Minor Scrapes: Chew or crush fresh clean broadleaf plantain leaves ('Nature's Bandage' growing in most yards) into a green poultice to draw out bee/mosquito sting itch and soothe minor cuts.

5. Earache / Swimmer's Ear Prevention: Mix 1:1 white vinegar and 70% rubbing alcohol—put 3 drops in each ear after swimming to dry moisture and acidify against bacterial swimmer's ear (ONLY if eardrum is intact and no pain/drainage exists).
guides.safety: NEVER give honey to infants under 12 months old (risk of infant botulism), and never put drops in an ear with suspected eardrum rupture or severe pain.

guides.title: Wilderness Hygiene, Trench Foot, Ringworm & UTI Prevention
steps: Wash hands with soap and water (or 60%+ alcohol sanitizer) before EVERY meal prep and after every bathroom trip—fecal-oral transmission causes 80% of disaster camp outbreaks.
Perform a daily 'bird bath' wash of high-friction zones (armpits, groin, feet) and change into dry socks before bed to prevent fungal jock itch, athlete's foot, and immersion trench foot.
Treat fungal ringworm/athlete's foot early with topical clotrimazole or terbinafine twice daily for 2 full weeks (continuing 7 days after rash clears).
Prevent urinary tract infections (UTIs) during travel/outages by staying well hydrated, never holding urine for hours, and wiping front-to-back.
guides.safety: Keep a separate dedicated 'sick tent/room' and utensils for anyone with vomiting or diarrhea.

guides.title: Emergency Dental Care: Toothache, Lost Filling & Abscess Relief
steps: Lost Filling or Broken Tooth: Rinse gently with warm salt water, dry the cavity with a cotton swab, roll a pea-sized ball of temporary zinc-oxide dental putty (DenTemp), press into the cavity, and bite down gently to shape.

Severe Toothache Nerve Pain: Dip a tiny cotton pellet in clove oil (natural eugenol anesthetic), dab ONLY onto the aching tooth cavity (avoid gums, as pure clove oil stings soft tissue), and take ibuprofen + acetaminophen together.
Loose Crown: Clean inside the crown, coat with temporary dental cement (NEVER superglue!), and press firmly back onto the tooth.
guides.safety: Facial cheek swelling, fever, or difficulty swallowing indicates a spreading dental abscess requiring urgent dentist/ER antibiotics.

guides.title: Food Poisoning vs. Botulism Warning Signs
steps: Standard food poisoning (Staph, Salmonella, Norovirus): Focus on aggressive oral rehydration (ORS sips every 5–10 minutes), rest the gut with bland foods (bananas, rice, applesauce, toast) once vomiting stops for 6 hours.
Avoid anti-diarrheal loperamide (Imodium) if you have a high fever or bloody diarrhea, as slowing the gut traps invasive bacteria inside.

BOTULISM EMERGENCY RED FLAGS (from improperly home-canned low-acid foods or bulging cans): Descending paralysis starting 12–36 hours later—double/blurry vision, drooping eyelids, slurred speech, dry mouth, difficulty swallowing, and muscle weakness—call 911 immediately for botulinum antitoxin.
guides.safety: Never taste-test questionable home-canned vegetables or meats—botulinum toxin is odorless and tasteless.

guides.title: Solo & Two-Person Emergency Carries & Improvised Blanket Litter
supplies: Heavy blanket, tarp, or two buttoned jackets
steps: Solo Ankle/Shoulder Drag (short distance out of immediate fire/traffic danger): Grasp clothing behind the shoulders (supporting head on your forearms) or grasp ankles and pull straight along the spine's axis.
Two-Person Fore-and-Aft Carry: Stronger rescuer stands behind patient reaching under armpits to clasp wrists across chest; second rescuer stands between patient's legs lifting behind knees.

Improvised Blanket Stretcher: Lay a heavy blanket flat, place Pole #1 one-third across and fold the short flap over it, place Pole #2 on top of the folded edge two-thirds across, and fold the remaining blanket over Pole #2—body weight locks the friction folds tightly.
guides.safety: Test every improvised stretcher with a healthy volunteer before lifting an injured person, and lift with legs—not your back.

guides.title: Master Home & Vehicle Trauma + OTC Medicine Cabinet Checklist
supplies: Steri-Strips, non-stick pads, hydrocolloid bandages, medical tape
Acetaminophen, Ibuprofen, Aspirin 325 mg, Diphenhydramine (Benadryl), Cetirizine, Loperamide, Bismuth, Hydrocortisone 1%, Bacitracin, Clotrimazole, ORS packets, White vinegar, Clove oil
steps: Divide medical gear into two distinct layers: (1) an exterior quick-pull Trauma Pouch (tourniquet, hemostatic gauze, pressure bandage, shears, gloves) reachable in 3 seconds, and (2) an organized Boo-Boo & OTC Medicine kit.
Label medication bottles with adult dosing and expiration dates, rotating OTC meds every 12–18 months.
Keep a laminated card inside listing family allergies, blood types, current prescriptions, and Poison Control (1-800-222-1222).
guides.safety: Store medicines in a cool, dry interior closet—high heat in car trunks or garages degrades epinephrine, aspirin, and liquid gels rapidly.

guides.title: Pet First Aid: Cat & Dog Wounds, Heatstroke, Toxins & CPR
gear: Soft muzzle or gauze strip (for injured dogs)
supplies: Hydrogen peroxide 3% (ONLY for dogs under vet direction—NEVER cats!)
steps: Safe Restraint: Wrap an injured cat snugly in a thick bath towel ('purrito') leaving only the injured paw/head exposed; even gentle pets bite when terrified or in pain.
Bleeding & Paw Cuts: Apply direct pressure with sterile gauze and wrap with self-adhering vet wrap (leave two middle toes visible to check for swelling/coldness).
Pet Heatstroke (panting excessively, bright red gums, drooling, staggering): Move to AC immediately, wet fur with cool (not ice-cold) water, point a fan on them, and transport to an emergency vet.

DEADLY HOUSEHOLD PET TOXINS (especially toxic to cats!): Lilies (even pollen or vase water causes fatal kidney failure in cats), Acetaminophen/Tylenol (fatal to cats!), Ibuprofen, Onions/Garlic, Grapes/Raisins, Xylitol sweetener, Chocolate, and Permethrin flea products.
guides.safety: NEVER give human painkillers (Tylenol, Advil, Aleve, Aspirin) to cats—a single regular Tylenol tablet is fatal to a cat.

guides.title: 911 / Search & Rescue Medical Report (MIST Handover Card)
steps: Write down a concise MIST report before calling 911 or handing a patient off to paramedics/SAR so critical details aren't forgotten under stress:
M — Mechanism of Injury / Illness (e.g., fall from 10 ft ladder, stingray sting, chest pain at 2:15 PM).
I — Injuries Found (head-to-toe list, plus exact tourniquet application time).
S — Signs & Vitals (alertness level, pulse rate, breathing rate, skin color/temp, blood pressure/temp if measured).
T — Treatment Given (pressure bandage, EpiPen given at 2:20 PM, 325 mg aspirin chewed, hot water soak).
guides.safety: Always send someone to the street or trailhead with a flashlight/bright vest to flag down arriving ambulances.

guides.title: Portuguese Man-of-War vs. Sea Nettle vs. Fire Coral Stings
steps: Portuguese Man-of-War (floating blue/purple gas bladder with long trailing tentacles common on Galveston beaches): Rinse first with SEAWATER (note: vinegar can trigger nematocyst discharge in some Physalia species—if in doubt, rinse gently with seawater, pluck tentacles with tweezers, then immerse in 110°F–113°F hot water for 30 minutes).
True Jellyfish (Sea Nettles, Moon Jellies, Box Jellies): Flood with household white vinegar for 30 seconds first to lock nematocysts, scrape gently with a credit card, then soak in hot water.
Fire Coral & Hydroids (snorkeling/reef scrapes): Rinse with vinegar or seawater, wash with soap/water, apply 1% hydrocortisone cream, and watch closely for marine bacterial infection.
guides.safety: Never rub sand onto a jellyfish sting or rinse with tap water/bottled drinking water—freshwater causes remaining stingers to fire.

guides.title: Sea Lice (Seabather's Eruption) & Swimmer's Itch Relief
steps: Seabather's Eruption ('sea lice' — microscopic jellyfish larvae trapped inside swimwear in warm Gulf/Caribbean surf): Remove swimsuit BEFORE showering in freshwater (freshwater bursts trapped larvae under fabric).
Wash skin thoroughly with soap and water, and machine-wash swimwear in hot water with detergent before re-wearing (air-drying leaves live stinging cells in fabric).
Soothe itchy red bumps under swimsuit lines with 1% hydrocortisone cream, calamine lotion, and oral cetirizine or diphenhydramine.
guides.safety: Rinse off promptly at beach showers after removing swimwear rather than sitting in wet suits for hours.

guides.title: Toxic Plant Ingestion: Oleander, Sago Palm, Nightshade & Mushrooms
steps: Gulf Coast Backyard Killers to know: Oleander (all parts contain cardiac glycosides), Sago Palm (seeds/nuts cause severe liver failure in people and dogs), Castor Bean (ricin), Angel's Trumpet / Jimsonweed (anticholinergic delirium), and Wild Mushrooms.

If someone chews or swallows an unknown berry, leaf, or mushroom: sweep remaining plant pieces out of the mouth, rinse mouth with water, save a stem/leaf/cap in a bag for botanical ID, and call Poison Control (1-800-222-1222) immediately.
Do NOT wait for symptoms to appear—liver-toxic mushrooms (Death Cap / Destroying Angel) cause delayed organ damage 12–24 hours after eating.
guides.safety: Never induce vomiting unless explicitly instructed by Poison Control.

guides.title: Household Chemical Poisoning: Bleach + Ammonia / Acid Gas & Cleaners
supplies: 4–8 oz cool water or milk (ONLY if awake, alert, and advised by Poison Control)
steps: Bleach Mixed with Ammonia or Toilet Bowl Acid: Produces toxic chloramine or chlorine gas—evacuate the bathroom/room immediately, close the door, turn on exhaust/open exterior windows from outside, and breathe fresh air.

Swallowed Corrosive Cleaners (drain cleaner, oven cleaner, bleach, laundry pods): Do NOT induce vomiting and do NOT give charcoal; if alert with no trouble swallowing, give small sips of water/milk ONLY if directed by Poison Control, and go to the ER for airway/esophageal evaluation.
guides.safety: Never mix chlorine bleach with vinegar, toilet bowl cleaners, or ammonia.

guides.title: Leech, Centipede, Millipede & Blister Beetle Exposure Remedies
steps: Leech Removal: Slide a fingernail or credit card edge flat against the skin under the small head sucker first, then the rear sucker—NEVER burn leeches with a lighter, pour salt, or yank straight off (which causes them to vomit gut bacteria into the wound). Expect harmless oozing for hours due to natural hirudin anticoagulant.
Giant Texas Centipede Bite: Wash thoroughly, soak in warm/hot water or apply a cool compress, and take oral pain relievers/antihistamines.
Millipede & Blister Beetle Skin Contact: Wash skin immediately with soap and water (do NOT crush blister beetles on skin—cantharidin fluid raises painful chemical blisters).
guides.safety: Apply firm direct pressure with sterile gauze over oozing leech bites until clotting completes.

guides.title: Opioid / Fentanyl Overdose Recognition & Narcan (Naloxone) Rescue
steps: Recognize opioid overdose triad: unresponsive to firm sternal rub, slow/absent breathing (<8 breaths/min) or snoring/gurgling 'death rattle', and pinpoint pupils with bluish lips/fingernails.
Call 911 immediately, tilt head back, insert the Narcan nasal nozzle fully into one nostril, and press the plunger firmly (do NOT prime/test spray first—each unit is single-dose).
Start rescue breathing / CPR immediately while waiting 2–3 minutes for Narcan to take effect; if breathing does not return after 2–3 minutes, give a second Narcan dose in the OTHER nostril.
guides.safety: Narcan wears off in 30–90 minutes while long-acting opioids remain in the body—never leave the person alone after they wake up.

guides.title: Seizure First Aid: Protecting the Head & When to Call 911
steps: Ease the person gently to the floor, clear hard/sharp furniture away, and cushion their head with a folded jacket or pillow.
Roll them onto their side (recovery position) as soon as possible so saliva drains out of the mouth.
STRICTLY DO NOT: put anything in their mouth (people cannot swallow their tongue, and spoons/fingers break teeth or get bitten) and do NOT hold their arms/legs down.
Time the seizure: call 911 if convulsions last longer than 5 minutes, a second seizure follows immediately, it is their first-ever seizure, or it occurred in water.
guides.safety: Stay calmly with the person afterward during the confused, sleepy 'post-ictal' recovery phase.

guides.title: Asthma Attack & Hyperventilation / Panic Attack Differentiation
steps: Asthma Attack (audible wheezing on exhale, chest tightness, tripod sitting posture, trouble speaking full sentences): Help the person sit upright leaning slightly forward, shake their Albuterol rescue inhaler, attach a spacer if available, and give 2 puffs spaced 30–60 seconds apart (up to 4 puffs every 20 minutes while awaiting EMS).

Panic / Hyperventilation Attack (rapid shallow chest breathing, tingling fingers/lips, chest tightness, NO wheezing): Coach slow boxed breathing—inhale through nose for 4 seconds, hold 2 seconds, exhale slowly through pursed lips for 6 seconds (do NOT breathe into a paper bag, which risks dangerous hypoxia).
guides.safety: Silent chest (no air moving at all during a severe asthma attack) or blue lips means imminent respiratory arrest—call 911 immediately.

guides.title: Pelvic Binder & Femur Fracture Field Stabilization
gear: SAM Pelvic Sling or wide bedsheet/tarp strip
steps: Suspect pelvic fracture after high-speed crash or fall from height if hips feel unstable or painful on gentle inward press: wrap a wide folded bedsheet or commercial pelvic sling tightly around the GREATER TROCHANTERS (hip bones, NOT the high waist) and tie/clamp snug to close open-book pelvic bleeding.
Tie knees and ankles gently together with padded cravats to prevent outward leg rotation.
For a mid-thigh femur break: pad between the legs and splint from armpit to ankle on the outside and groin to ankle on the inside.
guides.safety: Pelvic and femur fractures can hide 1.5–3 liters of internal blood loss—treat aggressively for shock and evacuate urgently.

guides.title: Snow Blindness (UV Keratitis) & Welder's Flash Eye Relief
gear: Dark wrap-around sunglasses or improvised cardboard/bark slit goggles
steps: Prevent UV corneal sunburn on bright snow, water, or white sand by wearing UV-blocking sunglasses or cutting narrow horizontal slits in duct tape/cardboard.

If gritty burning eye pain, tearing, and light sensitivity strike 6–12 hours after bright UV exposure: remove contact lenses immediately, rest in a completely dark room/tent with cool moist cloths over closed eyelids, use preservative-free artificial tears, and take oral ibuprofen.
Corneal cells usually regenerate within 24–48 hours.
guides.safety: Never use topical anesthetic eye drops repeatedly—they prevent corneal healing and cause permanent ulcers.

guides.title: Sunburn, Heat Rash (Prickly Heat) & Chafing Remedies
supplies: Plain petroleum jelly / zinc oxide diaper cream
steps: Sunburn: Take ibuprofen within the first 6 hours to blunt UV skin inflammation, take a cool shower, apply pure fragrance-free aloe vera gel or moisturizing lotion while skin is damp, and drink extra water.

Heat Rash (Prickly Heat — tiny red bumps in sweaty folds): Move to AC/fan airflow, cool skin with wet cloths, wear loose breathable cotton/linen, and dust lightly with plain cornstarch (avoid heavy greasy ointments that block sweat ducts).
Inner-Thigh / Underarm Chafing: Wash gently with cool water, pat dry, and apply a barrier layer of zinc oxide cream or plain petroleum jelly.
guides.safety: Seek medical care if sunburn develops large blisters over >20% of the body, fever, chills, or nausea ('sun poisoning').

guides.title: Kidney Stone vs. Appendicitis Abdominal Pain Triage
steps: Appendicitis Red Flags: Pain starting dull around the belly button that migrates over 6–24 hours to the LOWER RIGHT abdomen (McBurney's point), worsens with coughing, bumps, or jumping on heels, accompanied by loss of appetite, nausea, and low-grade fever.
Kidney Stone Pattern: Sudden waves of severe flank/back pain radiating down toward the groin, restlessness (unable to lie still), nausea, and pink/red urine.
For suspected appendicitis: keep the person NPO (nothing to eat or drink in case surgery is needed), do NOT apply heating pads (heat increases rupture risk), and transport to an ER immediately.
guides.safety: Rigid 'board-like' belly muscles or severe pain when releasing pressure (rebound tenderness) signals surgical peritonitis.

guides.title: Constipation, Heartburn / GERD & Acid Reflux Field Remedies
steps: Acute Heartburn / Acid Reflux: Dissolve 1/2 teaspoon baking soda in 4 oz water for fast temporary neutralization, chew calcium carbonate antacids, avoid lying flat for 3 hours after eating, and elevate head/torso on an incline.

Disaster / Travel Constipation (common when switching to dry rations): Increase water intake + electrolytes first, eat prunes/dried apricots/oats, take psyllium fiber with a full glass of water, or use osmotic polyethylene glycol (MiraLAX).
guides.safety: Never confuse upper-abdominal heartburn with a heart attack—if chest pressure radiates to arm/jaw or causes sweating/shortness of breath, treat as cardiac.

guides.title: Sinus Congestion, Ear Barotrauma & Steam Inhalation Relief
supplies: Saline nasal rinse / Neti pot (distilled/boiled water ONLY)
steps: Steam Tent: Pour steaming hot water into a bowl, drape a bath towel over your head and the bowl, and breathe deeply through the nose for 10 minutes to thin thick sinus mucus.
Saline Nasal Irrigation: Flush sinuses using ONLY distilled, sterile, or previously boiled-and-cooled water mixed with buffered saline packets—NEVER straight tap water.
Limit oxymetazoline (Afrin) nasal spray to 3 consecutive days max to avoid rebound congestion.
guides.safety: CRITICAL: Never use unboiled tap water in a Neti pot or nasal rinse due to rare brain-eating amoeba (Naegleria fowleri) risk in warm climates.

guides.title: Sprained Back, Muscle Spasms & Sciatica Acute Relief
steps: After lifting heavy storm debris or sandbags, lie flat on your back on a firm floor with calves elevated at 90° on a chair seat ('psoas position') for 15 minutes to unload lumbar discs.
Use ice packs for 15–20 minutes during the first 48 hours to calm acute inflammation, then switch to moist heat to relax tight muscle spasms.
Take short, gentle 5-minute walks on flat ground every few hours rather than strict bedrest, which stiffens back muscles.
guides.safety: Numbness in the groin/saddle area or sudden loss of bowel/bladder control with back pain is Cauda Equina Syndrome—a surgical emergency.

guides.title: Splinter, Glass & Embedded Cactus Spine Extraction
supplies: White school glue (PVA) or duct tape (for fine cactus glochids)
steps: Fine Cactus Glochids or Fiberglass Fibers: Spread a thin coat of white Elmer's school glue over the area, let dry completely, and peel off in one sheet (or press duct tape gently and peel) to pull out hundreds of invisible hair-like spines at once.

Wood/Glass Splinters: Wipe skin and needle/tweezers with 70% alcohol, gently lift the thin roof skin over the splinter tip with the sterile needle parallel to the skin, and pull the splinter out at the exact angle it entered.
guides.safety: Never squeeze a glass splinter straight down—it shatters deeper into tissue.

guides.title: Making Medicinal Herbal Salves, Poultices & Tinctures at Home
gear: Double boiler / heatproof jar in saucepan
supplies: Dried calendula, plantain, or comfrey leaves
steps: Herbal Infused Oil: Simmer 1/2 cup dried calendula or plantain leaves in 1 cup olive oil over a gentle water bath (120°F–140°F) for 2 hours, then strain through butter muslin.

Healing Skin Salve: Melt 1 oz beeswax pastilles into the warm strained herbal oil (ratio: 1 oz beeswax per 1 cup oil), pour into clean tins, and cool uncovered—soothes chapped hands, minor scrapes, and dry heels.

Alcohol Tincture (shelf-stable 5+ years): Fill a jar halfway with chopped dried herbs (echinacea, ginger, elderberry, chamomile), cover completely with 80-proof vodka, shake daily for 4 weeks in a dark cabinet, and strain into dropper bottles.
guides.safety: Use comfrey salves ONLY on closed bruises/sprains—never on deep open puncture wounds, as rapid surface healing can trap bacteria inside.

guides.title: Natural Mosquito, Tick & Chigger Repellents + Bite Itch Stoppers
supplies: Oil of Lemon Eucalyptus (OLE / PMD) or Picaridin / DEET
steps: For high-disease-risk Gulf Coast mosquitoes (West Nile, Dengue) and ticks, use EPA-proven repellents: Picaridin (20%), DEET (20%–30%), or plant-based Oil of Lemon Eucalyptus (30% OLE—not plain lemon eucalyptus essential oil).
Treat outer hiking socks, boots, and pant cuffs with 0.5% Permethrin spray and let dry completely before wearing (kills ticks on contact for 6 washes; keep wet permethrin away from cats until dry!).
Stop mosquito bite itch instantly: press the back of a metal spoon warmed in hot tap water (120°F — warm, NOT scalding) onto the fresh bite for 10 seconds to denature histamine proteins.
guides.safety: Keep liquid permethrin strictly away from cats while wet; once fully dried on fabric, it is safe.

guides.title: Stye, Pink Eye (Conjunctivitis) & Blocked Tear Duct Care
steps: Eyelid Stye (tender red bump at lash line): Apply a clean warm damp washcloth compress to the closed eyelid for 10–15 minutes, 4 times daily, to unclog the oil gland—NEVER squeeze or pop a stye.
Viral/Bacterial Pink Eye: Wash hands constantly, use separate towels/pillowcases, wipe crust gently from inner corner outward with warm damp cotton, and discard eye makeup.
guides.safety: Seek prompt eye-doctor care if vision blurs, severe eye pain develops, or you wear contact lenses.

guides.title: Ingrown Toenail & Subungual Hematoma (Smashed Fingernail) Relief
steps: Mild Ingrown Toenail: Soak foot in warm Epsom salt water for 15 minutes, gently lift the corner of the nail, tuck a tiny wisp of cotton or waxed dental floss underneath to guide nail growth above the skin edge, and trim toenails straight across (never rounded).

Throbbing Blood Under Smashed Nail (Subungual Hematoma — within 24 hours): Clean nail with alcohol, heat the tip of an unbent paperclip red-hot in a flame (or spin a sterile needle tip gently), and melt/drill a tiny pinhole straight down through the center of the dark nail bed—trapped blood spurts out and throbbing pain stops instantly.
guides.safety: Do NOT attempt nail trephination if the finger is broken or if you have diabetes/poor circulation.

guides.title: Scalp Lacerations & Facial Wound Bleeding Control
steps: Scalp cuts bleed dramatically even when minor due to dense blood vessels—stay calm and press a thick stack of sterile gauze firmly directly onto the cut for 10 full minutes.
Before pressing hard on a head wound, feel gently around the edges first to make sure there is no soft, spongy depression indicating an underlying skull fracture.
Wrap an elastic bandage horizontally around the forehead/occiput (above ears and eyebrows) to hold the gauze pad in place.
guides.safety: Any head blow followed by dizziness, memory gap, or vomiting requires hospital CT evaluation.

guides.title: Amputated Finger / Part Preservation for Surgical Reattachment
steps: Control stump bleeding first with direct pressure, elevation, and a tourniquet only if arterial bleeding won't stop.
Rinse the severed finger/part gently with clean saline/water (do NOT scrub), wrap it in damp sterile gauze, and seal it inside a watertight zip-top bag.
Place that sealed bag INSIDE a second bag filled with ice and cold water—NEVER put the severed tissue directly on bare ice or submerged loose in water, which freezes and destroys cells.
guides.safety: Transport both the patient and the cooled part to a trauma/hand-surgery center immediately (viable window is 6–12+ hours when properly cooled).

guides.title: Croup, Whooping Cough & Nighttime Barking Cough Steam Protocol
steps: Viral Croup (seal-like barking cough in young children, worse at night): Sit with the child in a steam-filled bathroom with the hot shower running for 10 minutes, then step outside into cool night air (or open the freezer door for 2 minutes)—alternating warm mist and cool air shrinks airway swelling fast.
Keep the child calm and upright—crying tightens narrowed vocal cords.
guides.safety: Call 911 immediately if the child makes high-pitched squeaking noises while breathing IN at rest (stridor), drools unable to swallow, or sucks skin in between ribs.

guides.title: Checking Vital Signs Without Electronic Monitors (Pulse, Breathing, Skin, Pupils)
steps: Pulse Rate & Quality: Press index and middle fingers (never your thumb) lightly on the radial wrist pulse (thumb side) or carotid neck pulse; count beats for 30 seconds and double (normal resting adult = 60–100 bpm; note if strong/bounding vs. weak/thready).
Respiratory Rate: Watch chest rise silently for 30 seconds and double without telling the patient (normal adult = 12–20 breaths/min; >24 or <8 is abnormal).
Capillary Refill & Skin: Squeeze a fingernail bed white for 2 seconds and release—pink color should return in under 2 seconds; feel forehead with back of hand for fever/clamminess.
Pupils (PERRL): Shine a penlight briefly from the side into each eye—both pupils should be equal in size and constrict briskly.
guides.safety: Record vitals every 15 minutes in unstable patients—a rising pulse combined with falling skin temperature is the earliest warning of hidden shock.

guides.title: Disaster Psychological First Aid: Calming Panic & Acute Stress
steps: Use the 5-4-3-2-1 Sensory Grounding technique to pull someone out of an acute panic spiral: name 5 things you can see, 4 things you can physically touch, 3 things you can hear, 2 things you can smell, and 1 thing you can taste.

Give panicked bystanders a concrete, simple, helpful task (holding a flashlight, timing a bandage, organizing water bottles)—purposeful action immediately restores prefrontal control over amygdala panic.
Keep children close to familiar routines, give honest age-appropriate reassurance, and limit repetitive disaster radio/news loops.
guides.safety: Never dismiss severe chest pain or shortness of breath as 'just anxiety' until physical causes are ruled out.

cat / sof-t windlass tourniquet.def: A heavy-duty 1.5-inch-wide limb strap with an internal tightening band, rigid windlass twisting rod, locking clip, and time tag designed to completely occlude arterial blood flow in a severely injured arm or leg within seconds.

sam splint.def: A lightweight, waterproof thin core of soft aluminum sandwiched between closed-cell foam. Flat when rolled in a pack, it becomes rigid enough to immobilize broken arms, legs, or ankles once curved into a C-gutter or T-fold.

hemostatic gauze.def: Z-folded sterile medical gauze impregnated with natural mineral kaolin or shellfish-derived chitosan that accelerates the body's clotting cascade on contact when packed tightly into deep arterial wounds.

vented commercial chest seal.def: An extra-sticky hydrogel adhesive dressing with one-way exhaust channels applied over penetrating chest wounds to prevent outside air from collapsing the lung while letting trapped internal air escape.

trauma shears.def: Angled stainless-steel medical scissors with a flattened, rounded safety tip designed to slide safely against skin while cutting swiftly through heavy denim, leather boots, seatbelts, and bandages.

epinephrine auto-injector.def: A spring-loaded single-dose syringe delivering intramuscular epinephrine into the outer mid-thigh to rapidly reverse airway swelling and blood-pressure collapse during life-threatening anaphylaxis.
